en.title: History and International Studies: the whole course
en.short: What history and international studies cover, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
History and International Studies is a combined field. History asks how people lived, why things changed and how we know. International studies asks how states, peoples, firms and organisations relate across borders. The degree joins the two because no country’s past can be understood alone. Trade, migration, empire, war, diplomacy and law have always crossed frontiers.

The subject teaches you to read evidence critically, explain change over time and compare societies without assuming one is normal. It also teaches you to describe institutions and rules, such as treaties and international organisations, and to ask who benefits from them. Graduates work in teaching, research, archives, museums, civil service, diplomacy, journalism, development work and NGOs.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Lengths and awards differ, so check your own student handbook. In Nigeria, a full-time BA in History and International Studies commonly takes four years; direct entry may shorten it. Some departments teach history and international studies together, while others offer separate degrees with shared courses. In the United Kingdom, a full-time bachelor’s in history or international relations commonly takes three years, except in Scotland where it is four years. In the United States, four years is common.

The early years usually give a foundation in historical method and world history. Later years add regional history, international relations, law and organisations, and a research project. In Nigeria, the National Universities Commission regulates university programmes, but the details of each programme are set by the university. Always check the current handbook for course titles, credit units, prerequisites and graduation requirements.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory courses teach what history is, how historians have written it, and how sources become evidence. You learn chronology and periodisation, philosophy of history, oral tradition and oral history, archaeology and material culture, and quantitative and digital methods. These tools matter because every later topic depends on evidence and interpretation.

Core courses then move through time and space. They cover African prehistory, ancient civilisations of Africa and Asia, the classical Mediterranean, the rise of Islamic civilisation, and African kingdoms and states to 1800. They examine the Atlantic slave trade, European overseas expansion, the early modern world and the Industrial Revolution. Next come colonialism and imperialism, African resistance, colonial economy and society, nationalism and independence, Nigerian history, and postcolonial Africa.

The international studies side runs alongside this. It includes the two World Wars and the interwar world, the Cold War and after, the history of international relations and diplomacy, foreign policy of African states, international organisations, public international law, international political economy and development, and peace, conflict and security studies. A research methods course prepares the long essay. Master’s work adds advanced historiography, dissertation design and a specialist seminar.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Read with a question in mind. For each topic, identify the main claim, the evidence used and the strongest objection. Make a timeline of names, dates and events, but do not stop there. Explain causes, connections and consequences in your own words.

Practise source criticism. For every document, ask who made it, when, for whom and why. Compare two accounts of the same event. In oral history, record who was interviewed, the place, the date and the language, and treat memory as evidence that needs checking.

Use the library and official archives. Learn the citation style your department requires. Keep a running list of references. For international topics, check the current official source for treaties, memberships and rules, because these change. Join study groups for debate, but write alone.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Many students reduce history to memorising dates. Dates help, but explanation and evidence carry the marks. Others judge the past only by present values, or assume that one country’s experience stands for all. Africa is not one story, and neither is Europe.

A common error is to treat a source as neutral. Every source has a purpose and a silence. Another is to quote a law, treaty or organisation without naming the country or the date. International law and institutions change, and so do their members.

In research, students often choose a topic too broad to answer, or make a claim that their evidence cannot support. Plagiarism, missing references and copying lecture notes without reading are serious. Finally, do not confuse international relations with news commentary. The subject asks for evidence, theory and historical context.

keyPoints: History and International Studies combines evidence about the past with the study of relations across borders.
Every historical claim depends on sources, and every source must be questioned.
Degree lengths, awards and course rules differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Study the main areas in order: method, world and African history, then international relations and law.
Explain causes and consequences rather than memorising dates alone.
Name the country and date when you state a law, treaty or institution rule.

en.title: History as a Discipline: Nature, Scope and Uses
en.short: Defines history, separates it from the past and myth, explains its uses, and introduces auxiliary sciences.

sections.heading: What history is
sections.text: History is the disciplined study of the human past based on evidence. The past is everything that happened, including events no one recorded. History is not that whole past. It is the organised account historians build from surviving traces, and it changes when new evidence appears. A historian asks what happened, why, and how we know. This makes history an argument about evidence, not a list of dates.

sections.heading: History, myth and legend
sections.text: Myth and legend are stories that explain origins, identity or values. They may contain memory, but they are not tested against evidence in the way history is. A legend about a founding ancestor can be important to a community without being a historical record. Historians treat such stories as evidence of belief and memory, not as direct fact. They compare them with other sources before drawing conclusions.

sections.heading: Why societies study it
sections.text: Societies study history to understand identity, change and human choices. It helps citizens judge public claims, recognise propaganda and see how institutions developed. It can inform policy, though the past never repeats exactly. It also supports reconciliation by explaining grievances. In a university, history trains careful reading, clear writing and the weighing of evidence.

sections.heading: Auxiliary sciences
sections.text: Auxiliary sciences are technical fields that help historians read evidence. Archaeology studies material remains such as buildings and tools. Epigraphy studies inscriptions on stone or metal. Numismatics studies coins, which can date trade and rulers. Chronology places events in order and assigns dates. Suppose a family in Ibadan keeps an old brass vessel. A historian may compare its style with dated pieces, read any inscription, and use chronology to place it in a period. The object alone does not tell the whole story; it must be interpreted with other evidence.

keyPoints: History is an evidence-based account of the human past, not the past itself.
Myth and legend may preserve memory but are not tested historical evidence.
Societies study history for identity, critical judgement, policy and reconciliation.
Archaeology, epigraphy, numismatics and chronology are auxiliary sciences.
Auxiliary sciences help date and interpret evidence but do not replace historical argument.

en.title: Historiography: How History Has Been Written
en.short: From chronicles to critical scholarship: European, Islamic and African ways of writing history.

sections.heading: What historiography is
sections.text: Historiography has two linked meanings: the writing of history, and the study of how history has been written. It examines a historian’s questions, methods, evidence and assumptions. A chronicle simply lists events in time order. Critical history tests claims, explains why things happened and states its argument openly. The writer’s standpoint matters because no historian can include everything. Choices about what to ask, whose voices to trust and how to explain change shape the story told.

sections.heading: From chronicle to criticism
sections.text: Classical Greek writers such as Herodotus and Thucydides, in the fifth century BCE, wrote narrative histories that asked about causes. Medieval European chronicles, often kept by monks, arranged events by year and read them through a religious or moral frame. From the Renaissance, antiquarians collected and questioned documents. In the nineteenth century, Leopold von Ranke and others helped make history a university discipline based on archival research and source criticism. Modern scholarship adds footnotes, peer review and explicit debate about interpretation.

sections.heading: Three traditions
sections.text: These developments were not only European. Islamic historiography developed strong checks on reports through isnad criticism, the study of chains of transmission, especially in hadith scholarship. Al-Tabari wrote a large universal history, and Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah (fourteenth century) analysed social and political change. African traditions are plural: griots and oral historians preserved genealogies and praise poetry; Arabic chronicles recorded Sahelian states; and from the mid twentieth century academic historians combined oral and written sources. Each tradition had its own critical practices.

sections.heading: Why standpoint matters
sections.text: Standpoint shapes selection and explanation. Suppose a court chronicler calls a king’s war a divinely favoured victory, a colonial officer’s report calls the same war a rebellion, and a modern historian asks who paid the taxes that supplied the army. Each account may contain facts, but each answers a different question from a different position. Good historiography therefore asks not only what happened but who wrote the account, for whom, using which method, and what it leaves out.

keyPoints: Historiography is both the writing of history and the study of how it has been written.
Classical Greek historians asked about causes, while medieval chronicles often arranged events by year within a religious frame.
Modern critical history developed with archival research, source criticism and professional university discipline in the nineteenth century.
Islamic historiography used isnad criticism and produced works such as al-Tabari’s history and Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah.
African historical writing includes oral traditions, Arabic chronicles and academic history combining oral and written sources.
A historian’s standpoint shapes the questions asked, evidence chosen and explanation given.

en.title: Sources and Evidence in History
en.short: Primary and secondary sources, oral, written, material and visual evidence, and source criticism.

sections.heading: Primary and secondary
sections.text: Primary sources come from the period under study or from people who took part in it: a letter, a treaty, a photograph, a court record, a coin or an interview with a witness. Secondary sources interpret such material later: textbooks, journal articles and documentaries. The same item can change class with the question. A 1950s newspaper is primary for a study of colonial reporting and secondary for a study of an earlier war. Ask what question you are answering before labelling a source.

sections.heading: Kinds of evidence
sections.text: Evidence reaches historians in several forms. Oral evidence is spoken testimony, such as a recorded interview or a remembered account. Written evidence includes letters, minutes, newspapers and official records. Material evidence is physical: buildings, tools, coins and graves. Visual evidence is pictorial or recorded: maps, paintings, photographs and film. These forms overlap. A filmed interview is oral and visual. Each form has limits: memory fades, documents serve their writers, objects lose context, and images can be staged.

sections.heading: Testing a source
sections.text: Source criticism tests a source before you use it. Provenance asks who made it, where, when and how it survived. Purpose asks why it was made and for whom. Reliability asks whether the maker could know and whether the account is consistent. Corroboration checks the claim against independent sources. A single source can start a question, but a claim is stronger when several independent sources agree. Distinguish fact, inference and opinion in your notes.

sections.heading: A short case
sections.text: Imagine a student studies a market strike in colonial Accra. A colonial officer’s report is primary, but its purpose was to justify official action. A trader’s recorded interview is also primary, but memory may fade. A later article is secondary. The student checks provenance, compares the report with the interview and with a newspaper photograph, and corroborates the date and demands. Only then does the student claim that the strike happened and why.

keyPoints: Primary sources come from the period or participants; secondary sources interpret them later.
Classification depends on the historian’s question, not only on the document’s age.
Oral, written, material and visual evidence each have strengths and limits.
Source criticism tests provenance, purpose, reliability and corroboration.
Corroboration means comparing a claim with independent sources.
A claim should be stated only after the evidence has been tested.

en.title: Philosophy of History and Interpretation
en.short: The past versus history, theories of historical causation, objectivity, bias, progress and values.

sections.heading: Past and history
sections.text: The past is everything that happened. History is a reasoned account of part of that past, built from surviving evidence. The past cannot change; an account can be revised when evidence or questions change. A date alone is not history. History explains, connects and interprets. Every account selects, and selection is not automatically bias. It becomes bias when evidence is ignored or distorted.

sections.heading: Causes and schools
sections.text: Historians ask why events happened. Idealist views, associated with R. G. Collingwood, stress thought and intention: to understand an action, reconstruct the beliefs and reasons behind it. Materialist views, especially Karl Marx’s historical materialism, stress economic conditions, technology and class relations. Ideas are seen as shaped by material life. Other approaches stress institutions, geography, culture or chance. Most historians combine causes. Suppose a coastal town declined after trade routes shifted. A materialist may point to lost commerce and taxes; an idealist to rulers’ beliefs and prestige; a political historian to local conflict. Each claim must be tested against evidence.

sections.heading: Objectivity and bias
sections.text: Objectivity means judging claims by evidence and fair method, not personal preference. Complete neutrality is hard, because historians choose questions, sources and words. Bias is a slant that ignores or misreads evidence. Good practice states assumptions, uses sources from several sides, and separates evidence from inference. Values enter when historians judge, for example, whether colonial rule was beneficial. They should make the standard clear. Max Weber distinguished value-relevance, why a topic matters, from value-freedom, keeping personal values out of causal analysis.

sections.heading: Progress and interpretation
sections.text: The idea of progress holds that history moves toward improvement. Enlightenment thinkers often expected reason and freedom to advance. Critics reply that progress is uneven, can coexist with atrocity, and is not one line. Interpretations differ over whether history has a purpose. Some see patterns; others stress chance and human choice. Students should ask what evidence supports each claim and what values it assumes.

keyPoints: The past is all that happened; history is a selective, evidence-based account of it.
Idealist explanations stress beliefs and intentions; materialist explanations stress economic and social conditions.
Most historical explanation combines several causes and tests each against evidence.
Objectivity is a method of fair evidence use, not complete neutrality.
Bias appears when evidence is ignored or distorted; historians should state their assumptions.
Ideas of progress are interpretations, not facts, and should be argued with evidence.

en.title: Chronology, Periodisation and Historical Geography
en.short: How historians date events, divide time into periods, and use maps and geography.

sections.heading: Ordering time
sections.text:
Chronology is the arrangement of events in time. Absolute dating gives a date in a known system, such as a calendar year in BCE (Before Common Era) or CE (Common Era), or a scientific result such as a radiocarbon range. Relative dating places events in order without exact years. In stratigraphy, the study of layers, lower layers are usually older than upper layers.

If layer B holds a coin minted in 1500 CE, layer B cannot be older than 1500, and layer A above it is later still. A timeline draws this order on a line. Synchronology compares events in different places at the same time, asking what happened together.

sections.heading: Dividing the past
sections.text:
Periodisation divides the past into named blocks. Ancient, medieval and modern are common in European history; many textbooks treat the medieval period as roughly the fifth to the fifteenth century CE.

Such labels are choices, not natural facts. They depend on the historian’s question, region and evidence. A period that fits European dynasties may hide African, Asian or American experiences. Historians therefore name periods carefully and say whose chronology they use.

sections.heading: Historical geography
sections.text:
Historical geography studies how space, place, environment and boundaries shaped the past. Maps are arguments: they select what to show and what to leave out. Projection (how a round earth is drawn flat), scale, colour and borders all influence meaning.

A map of a river and its trade routes can support a claim that towns grew at crossings. A different map of rainfall or soil may explain farming. Always ask who made a map, for what purpose, and what it omits.

sections.heading: Reading claims
sections.text:
Use chronology, periodisation and geography together. A claim like “the medieval town grew because of the river” needs a dated sequence, a justified period label and a map that shows the river, the town and the trade route.

Check the evidence behind each part. Dates may be approximate; period labels may be contested; maps may be reconstructed. State limits plainly.

keyPoints: Chronology orders events in time; absolute dating gives calendar or scientific dates, while relative dating gives sequence.
Stratigraphy and finds such as dated coins can establish relative order, not always exact years.
Timelines show sequence; synchronology compares events across places at the same time.
Periodisation is a choice shaped by region, evidence and the historian’s question.
Ancient, medieval and modern are European conventions and should not be applied everywhere without explanation.
Historical geography treats maps as arguments shaped by projection, scale and selection.

en.title: Oral Tradition and Oral History
en.short: Oral tradition versus oral history: collection, transcription, evaluation and African practice.

sections.heading: Two kinds of evidence
sections.text: Oral tradition is the past passed down by word of mouth across generations, often in fixed forms such as genealogies, praise poems, epics and ritual sayings. Oral history is the recorded testimony of living people about what they remember or experienced. The two overlap: a recorded interview may contain old tradition. Oral tradition is collective and performed; oral history is usually a first-person interview created by a researcher. Neither is automatically true or false.

sections.heading: Collecting testimony
sections.text: Collecting oral evidence needs preparation. Learn the language or work with a named interpreter. Ask for consent from the speaker and, where required, from elders or the community. Record with good equipment, note the date, place, interviewer, language and who else was present. Ask open questions, let silences stand, and interview several people separately. In African settings, griots and clan historians may be specialists, but ordinary elders, women and young people hold memory. Record performance, song and gesture, not only words.

sections.heading: Transcription and tests
sections.text: Transcription turns speech into text and is already interpretation. Keep a verbatim record, add time codes, and mark pauses, laughter and unclear words. Translate carefully, keep the original language beside the translation, and check the transcript with the speaker. Then test the evidence. Compare it with independent sources: written records, archaeology, linguistics, other witnesses. Check internal consistency, the chain of transmission, the witness’s closeness to events, possible bias, and whether the story serves the teller’s interests. A plausible detail is not proof.

sections.heading: African practice and example
sections.text: Example: a fictional family in Kano says its founder arrived from Bornu three generations before British rule. The researcher records two elders separately, keeps the Hausa audio, transcribes and translates it, and notes disagreement over the date. The founder’s name appears in a praise poem and a land document; the date does not. The name is better supported than the date. In African practice, oral tradition often carries law, land rights and identity, so collection must respect community ownership and return copies.

keyPoints: Oral tradition is passed down across generations; oral history records living memory.
Collect with consent, in the original language, recording context and performance.
Transcription and translation are interpretive; keep the original and check with the speaker.
Test oral evidence by corroboration, consistency, transmission chain, bias and plausibility.
In African practice, griots and elders may hold specialist knowledge; respect community ownership.
A plausible detail is not proof; agreement across independent sources strengthens a claim.

en.title: Archaeology and Material Culture: Reading Past Life from Remains
en.short: Survey, excavation, stratigraphy, typology, dating and artefacts as evidence in African prehistory.

sections.heading: Survey and excavation
sections.text: Archaeology studies past human life through material remains, or material culture: the objects, buildings and landscapes people made and used. Survey finds sites, mostly without digging. It uses field walking, aerial photographs, satellite images, geophysics and small test pits, and records location, size and visible remains. Excavation removes soil in controlled units, often a grid, and records each context, meaning a layer or structure with a position and history. Digging destroys a site, so recording is essential. A team mapping a rock shelter in Nigeria might record hearths, potsherds and stone tools before lifting them.

sections.heading: Stratigraphy and typology
sections.text: Stratigraphy reads layers. In undisturbed ground, lower layers are usually older than upper ones, unless later digging has mixed them. A feature cut into a layer is later than that layer. Typology groups artefacts by shared form and style. Seriation arranges types by changing frequency to suggest a sequence. These are relative dating methods: they say what is older or younger, not a calendar year. Context is vital; an object without context loses much of its evidential value.

sections.heading: Dating methods
sections.text: Absolute dating gives approximate ages. Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14 in organic remains such as charcoal or bone. It works for roughly the last 50,000 years and needs calibration. Its half-life is about 5,730 years: if a sample keeps 50% of its original carbon-14, about one half-life has passed, 5,730 years. Potassium-argon dating suits old volcanic rock. Thermoluminescence can date burnt flint or pottery. Dendrochronology uses tree-ring sequences. Each method has limits and error ranges.

sections.heading: Reading African prehistory
sections.text: In much of Africa written records are late or absent, so archaeology carries the main evidence for early farming, iron working, trade and state formation. Great Zimbabwe’s stone walls and imported objects are read as evidence of a wealthy trading centre, not proof of a foreign builder. Artefacts show technology, diet, exchange and belief, but interpretation must fit site context and be tested against other evidence. Looting and unrecorded digging destroy that evidence.

keyPoints: Survey locates sites without digging, while excavation records contexts but destroys the site.
Stratigraphy and typology give relative dates, not calendar years.
Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14 in organic remains and needs calibration; its half-life is about 5,730 years.
Context gives artefacts evidential value; an object without context is much less useful.
Archaeology supplies key evidence for African prehistory where written records are late or absent.
Interpretations must be tested against several lines of evidence and must respect site context.

en.title: Quantitative and Digital Methods for Historians
en.short: Covers basic statistics, tables, charts, rates, digital archives and mapping for historical evidence.

sections.heading: Numbers and tables
sections.text:
Quantitative history uses numbers to test arguments, not to replace interpretation. A statistic summarises observations; a variable is a changing feature, such as population or price. Ask who counted, what was counted and what was omitted. A tax register may list only taxable adults, not the whole population.

Keep a table with one row per case and one column per variable. State units, currency and missing values. Distinguish nominal values, in current prices, from real values, adjusted for price change. A source note lets readers check.

sections.heading: Rates and charts
sections.text:
A rate makes comparison fair when totals differ. Population rate per 1,000 = events ÷ population × 1,000. Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Price index = current basket cost ÷ base basket cost × 100.

Worked example: a port exported 12,000 tonnes in 1910 and 18,000 in 1920. Change = 18,000 − 12,000 = 6,000 tonnes. Percentage change = 6,000 ÷ 12,000 × 100 = 50%. If one crop earned 4 million of 16 million total export earnings, its share = 4 ÷ 16 × 100 = 25%. Bar charts compare categories, line charts show time, pie charts show shares. Mean = sum ÷ count; median = middle ordered value. Label units and do not distort axes.

sections.heading: Digital archives and maps
sections.text:
Digital tools widen access but do not remove judgement. Search catalogues and digitised collections by keyword, date and place. Use quotation marks for exact phrases and Boolean operators AND, OR, NOT. Metadata, such as date, creator and catalogue number, helps judge relevance and origin. Optical character recognition (OCR) makes page images searchable but misreads old print, so check the image. Not all records are online.

Historical GIS, a geographic information system, links data to places. Georeferencing fits an old map to modern coordinates, but boundaries and names change. State a map’s date, scale and source. Numbers and maps support interpretation; they do not make it.

keyPoints: Quantitative history tests and sharpens arguments; it does not replace interpretation.
A table needs clear units, a source note and a row for each case.
Population rate per 1,000 = events ÷ population × 1,000.
Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100; trade share = part ÷ total × 100; price index = current basket cost ÷ base basket cost × 100.
Charts must label units and avoid distorted axes; mean = sum ÷ count, median = middle ordered value.
Digital archives need metadata checks and OCR verification; GIS maps need date, scale and source.

en.title: African Prehistory: Human Origins to the Iron Age
en.short: Human origins, African Stone Age, farming, herding, iron, and archaeology with linguistics.

sections.heading: Human origins
sections.text: Africa holds the earliest hominin fossils. A hominin is a member of the human lineage after it split from the chimpanzee line. Hadar in Ethiopia yielded the skeleton Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis), about 3.2 million years old. Laetoli in Tanzania has footprints about 3.6 million years old. Olduvai Gorge and Lake Turkana have early Homo fossils and stone tools. Sterkfontein in South Africa is rich in Australopithecus remains. Early Homo sapiens fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco are about 300,000 years old. Dates are approximate.

sections.heading: Stone Age
sections.text: African archaeologists divide the Stone Age into Early, Middle and Later. The Early Stone Age includes Oldowan choppers and flakes from about 2.6 million years ago, then Acheulean handaxes. The Middle Stone Age, from 300,000 years ago, has more varied tools. The Later Stone Age, from 40,000 years ago, includes fine blades, bone tools and rock art. Dates vary by region. Stone tools are the main evidence because other materials rarely survive.

sections.heading: Farming and iron
sections.text: Farming began in Africa independently. Sorghum, pearl millet, yams, teff and African rice were domesticated in different regions. Cattle, sheep and goats were herded in the Sahara and Nile Valley. Metallurgy is the working of metals. Iron smelting appears in West Africa in the first millennium BC, for example in the Nok culture of central Nigeria. In eastern Africa it appears by the last centuries BC, and in southern Africa in the first millennium AD. The Bantu expansion carried farming, pottery and iron working across much of the continent.

sections.heading: Archaeology and linguistics
sections.text: Archaeology and linguistics are combined to reconstruct these periods. Historical linguistics uses the comparative method to reconstruct proto-languages, the ancestral languages behind related ones. Reconstructed words can show what speakers knew, such as terms for cattle, crops or iron. In the Bantu case, reconstructed words for farming and pottery match archaeological evidence of early farming settlements. Iron-working terms point to a later spread of iron working. This supports the spread of Bantu-speaking farmers. The fit is not perfect, because languages can spread without mass migration. Scholars compare evidence.

keyPoints: Africa has the earliest known hominin fossils, including Australopithecus afarensis and early Homo sapiens.
African archaeologists divide the Stone Age into Early, Middle and Later, with dates that vary by region.
Farming began independently in Africa, herding spread through the Sahara and Nile Valley, and iron working appears in the first millennium BC in West Africa.
The Bantu expansion spread Bantu languages, farming, pottery and iron working across central, eastern and southern Africa.
Historical linguistics reconstructs proto-languages and their vocabulary, which can be compared with archaeological evidence.
Languages can spread without mass migration, so scholars combine and debate several kinds of evidence.

en.title: Ancient Civilisations of Africa and Asia
en.short: Nile states, Mesopotamia, Indus cities, Shang China and Nok West Africa: states, writing, religion and economy.

sections.heading: River states
sections.text: Ancient Egypt grew along the Nile, where floods supported farming and a centralised state under pharaohs. Kush, in Nubia to the south, was a separate Nile state with its own kings; at times it ruled Egypt. In Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and Euphrates, Sumerian city-states such as Uruk developed temple-centred government. The Indus region had planned cities, including Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, with grid streets and drains. Early China’s Shang state, in the Yellow River valley, had kings, bronze weapons and walled towns. A state means a centralised political organisation with rulers, officials and ways of collecting tribute.

sections.heading: Writing and belief
sections.text: Writing served administration, religion and memory. Egyptian hieroglyphs are picture-like signs; Mesopotamian cuneiform is wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay. Indus signs survive on seals but remain undeciphered. Shang oracle bones are animal bones heated to ask ancestors and gods for guidance; the cracks and inscriptions record royal questions. Religion was tied to state power: Egyptian pharaohs were sacred rulers, Mesopotamian temples served gods and stored wealth, and Shang kings mediated with ancestors. Ziggurats were stepped temple platforms in Mesopotamia.

sections.heading: Economy and exchange
sections.text: These economies rested on irrigated agriculture, especially grain, plus crafts and trade. Mesopotamian temples and palaces organised storage, weaving and metalwork. Indus cities traded through ports and overland routes; their seals suggest control of goods. Shang China used bronze ritual vessels and collected tribute in labour and produce. Long-distance trade moved materials such as timber, copper and precious stones, though the details differ by region and period.

sections.heading: Nok evidence
sections.text: West Africa’s Nok culture, in central Nigeria, is known from archaeology rather than writing. Excavations have found terracotta human and animal figures, iron-smelting furnaces and slag, and settlement remains. The figures show skilled clay work; iron-smelting remains show local metal production. Dates vary, but Nok is usually placed in the first millennium BCE. Because there are no Nok texts, historians rely on material evidence and must avoid reading later Nigerian states back into it.

keyPoints: Egypt and Kush were Nile states, and Kush at times ruled Egypt.
Mesopotamian city-states centred on temples, and cuneiform served administration and religion.
Indus cities show planning and trade, but their script remains undeciphered.
Shang China was a king-centred state using oracle bones and bronze ritual vessels.
Nok culture is known from terracotta figures and iron-smelting remains, not from texts.
These civilisations shared farming and trade but differed in writing, religion and state form.

en.title: The Classical Mediterranean: Greece and Rome
en.short: Greek city-states, Roman politics, law, economy, decline and classical legacy.

sections.heading: Greek city-states and ideas
sections.text: The polis was a self-governing city-state with its surrounding land. Greek poleis shared language and gods but never formed one state. Athens had a limited democracy: male citizens voted in the assembly and served on juries, but women, slaves and metics (resident foreigners) were excluded. Sparta mixed kings, elders and assembly. Plato and Aristotle asked what justice and the best constitution are. Aristotle classified constitutions by who rules and for whose benefit, calling rule by the many for the common good a polity and its corrupt form democracy.

sections.heading: Roman Republic and law
sections.text: Rome expanded from city-state to Mediterranean power by alliance and conquest. The Republic, traditionally founded in 509 BCE, balanced consuls, a Senate and popular assemblies. Conflict between patricians and plebeians produced the Twelve Tables, early written law, and tribunes to protect plebeians. Roman law grew through praetors, officials who issued remedies, and jurists who interpreted ius civile, law for citizens, and ius gentium, law common to all peoples, first used in cases involving foreigners. The Republic was not a Greek-style democracy: offices were unpaid and influence depended on wealth and patron-client ties.

sections.heading: Empire, decline and legacy
sections.text: Civil wars ended the Republic. Augustus became princeps in 27 BCE, and the Empire combined republican forms with one-man rule. Its economy rested on agriculture, slavery and Mediterranean trade, supported by roads, harbours and coinage. Emperors used Egyptian and North African grain to feed Rome and keep order. The western Empire faced military, fiscal and political pressures and its last emperor was deposed in 476 CE; the eastern Empire survived as Byzantium. Historians stress multiple causes, not one. The legacy includes Greek political thought, Roman law, citizenship, republicanism, Latin and civic architecture, which shaped later Europe and, through European empires, the world.

keyPoints: The polis was a self-governing city-state; Greek poleis shared culture but not a single state.
Athenian democracy was limited to male citizens, excluding women, slaves and metics.
The Roman Republic balanced consuls, Senate and assemblies, and its law grew through praetors and jurists.
The Empire under Augustus combined republican forms with one-man rule and relied on agriculture, slavery and trade.
The last western Roman emperor was deposed in 476 CE, but historians explain decline by multiple pressures, not one cause.
Classical Greek thought and Roman law shaped later European and world institutions.

en.title: The Rise of Islamic Civilisation: Caliphates, Trade and Learning
en.short: Islam’s rise, the caliphates, and Islamic trade and learning in Africa and beyond.

sections.heading: Muhammad and the caliphates
sections.text:
Islam began in Mecca, in the Arabian Peninsula, where Muhammad (about 570 to 632 CE) preached belief in one God. In 622 he and his followers moved to Medina; this migration, the Hijra, marks the start of the Islamic calendar. After his death in 632 the caliphs, or successors, led the community. The first four, the Rashidun, were followed by the Umayyads (661 to 750), ruling from Damascus, and the Abbasids (750 to 1258), who built Baghdad.

Later Muslim empires included the Ottomans, who took Constantinople in 1453, and the Mughals in India.

sections.heading: Conquest and conversion
sections.text: Arab armies took Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Persia within a generation, then North Africa and, from 711, Iberia. Non-Muslims who accepted Islamic rule, called dhimmi, kept their religion and paid a tax, jizya. Conversion was slow and uneven, and Sufi teachers and traders often spread the faith. Islam also travelled by sea along the East African coast, where Swahili city-states such as Kilwa grew rich on Indian Ocean trade.

sections.heading: Sahara and Sahel
sections.text: Across the Sahara, caravans linked West African gold and salt. Gold came from the Bambuk and Bure fields, salt from Saharan mines such as Taghaza. The empire of Ghana grew rich on this trade; Mali and Songhai followed it, and their rulers adopted Islam while older customs continued. Mansa Musa of Mali, on pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, gave away so much gold that its value fell in Cairo, later Arabic accounts report.

sections.heading: Centres of learning
sections.text: Scholarship flourished. In Baghdad’s House of Wisdom, translators put Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic; al-Khwarizmi worked on algebra, and Ibn Sina wrote a medical canon used for centuries. Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddimah on the rise and fall of states. In Africa, the Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez and al-Azhar in Cairo, founded in 970, became teaching centres, and Timbuktu’s Sankore mosque drew scholars such as Ahmad Baba.

keyPoints: The Hijra of 622 marks the start of the Islamic calendar; Muhammad died in 632.
The Rashidun, Umayyad (Damascus) and Abbasid (Baghdad) caliphates carried Islamic rule from Persia to Iberia and North Africa.
Dhimmi communities kept their faith and paid the jizya; conversion was gradual, not instant.
Trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt tied West Africa to the Mediterranean world and helped Islam spread in the Sahel.
Mali and Songhai adopted Islam while keeping older customs; Mansa Musa’s 1324 pilgrimage showed Mali’s wealth.
Baghdad, Fez, Cairo and Timbuktu were major centres of Islamic learning.

en.title: African Kingdoms and States to 1800
en.short: It covers Sahel empires, Yoruba and Benin states, Great Zimbabwe, Ethiopia and Kongo, plus politics, trade and belief.

sections.heading: Sahel empires
sections.text: Ghana, Mali and Songhai were Sahelian empires built on trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and slaves. Ghana’s king taxed trade and ruled through officials; al-Bakri’s Arabic account of 1068 describes its capital. Mali’s Mansa used provincial governors and promoted Islam; Ibn Battuta visited in 1352. Songhai’s Askia Muhammad strengthened Gao, Timbuktu and Djenne and employed Islamic scholars. Kanem Bornu’s Sefawa Mai ruled with a council and linked Lake Chad to North Africa. The Hausa city-states, including Kano and Katsina, had walled towns, kings called sarki, councils and markets; Islam grew from the fourteenth century.

sections.heading: Forest states
sections.text: Ife was a Yoruba city ruled by the Oni and known for brass and terracotta art. Oyo, its neighbour, was an empire led by the Alaafin with the Oyo Mesi council; its cavalry and trade in slaves, cloth and horses supported power. Benin was ruled by the Oba with chiefs and guilds; its brass plaques and walls are key evidence. These states combined kingship with councils, markets and indigenous religion, while Islam and later Christianity entered through trade and contact.

sections.heading: Southern kingdoms
sections.text: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a Shona state, its stone walls and imported goods showing gold and ivory trade with the Indian Ocean coast. Ethiopia’s Solomonic dynasty ruled through emperors, the Orthodox Church and provincial lords; manuscripts and rock-hewn churches, built by the earlier Zagwe dynasty, are evidence. Kongo’s Manikongo governed provinces and client chiefs, and from the late fifteenth century engaged Portuguese missionaries and traders. Christianity in Kongo mixed with local beliefs.

sections.heading: Evidence and belief
sections.text: Historians combine archaeology, oral tradition, Arabic chronicles, European accounts, inscriptions, art and architecture. These sources are uneven: Arabic writers often focused on rulers and trade, European accounts on coast and Christianity, and oral traditions on founding lineages. Belief systems included Islam in the Sahel, Christianity in Ethiopia and Kongo, and indigenous religions across all these states. Evidence must be read critically, because each source has its own purpose and limits.

keyPoints: Sahel empires depended on trans-Saharan trade and combined kingship with Islamic administration.
Mali and Songhai used provincial officials and Islamic scholarship, especially at Timbuktu.
Hausa city-states and Kanem Bornu linked Lake Chad and the savannah to North African trade.
Ife, Oyo and Benin combined kingship, councils and art with regional trade.
Great Zimbabwe, Ethiopia and Kongo show diverse state forms, from stone-built trade centres to Christian kingdoms.
Historians use archaeology, oral tradition, Arabic chronicles, European accounts, art and architecture, reading each critically.

en.title: The Atlantic Slave Trade: Origins, Plantations, Resistance and Effects
en.short: Routes, volume debates, plantation slavery, resistance, African effects and abolition.

sections.heading: Origins and routes
sections.text: Atlantic slavery grew from Portuguese voyages along West Africa in the fifteenth century and from sugar colonies in the Atlantic islands and Brazil. Europeans bought captives from African rulers and traders, then shipped them west. The so-called triangular trade was a pattern, not a fixed rule: European goods went to Africa, captives crossed the Atlantic in the Middle Passage, and colonial produce returned to Europe. Historians debate totals. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database suggests roughly 12.5 million embarked and about 10.7 million landed in the Americas, but estimates vary and should be checked against current scholarship.

sections.heading: Plantations and resistance
sections.text: Plantation slavery took root in Brazil, the Caribbean and the southern North American colonies. Sugar, tobacco, rice and later cotton were grown by enslaved people under chattel slavery, meaning people were treated as property. Conditions were brutal and mortality high. Resistance took many forms: shipboard revolts, flight to maroon communities of escaped slaves, sabotage, slowed work and cultural survival. Abolition came by stages. Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1833; France abolished slavery in 1848; the United States in 1865; Brazil in 1888. These dates are national, not universal.

sections.heading: Effects and debate
sections.text: Effects on Africa are disputed. The trade removed millions of people, created insecurity and encouraged slave-raiding states, and changed gender and labour patterns. Some historians argue it deepened African poverty. Eric Williams (1944) linked Caribbean slavery and the slave trade to British industrial growth; Joseph Inikori later defended a strong African and Atlantic role. Seymour Drescher and others reply that British growth had wider causes and that abolition had moral and political roots. The debate is not settled. A concrete case is the Kingdom of Dahomey, whose rulers sold captives and fought wars that supplied the trade, showing African agency and complicity, not simple victimhood.

keyPoints: The Atlantic slave trade grew from fifteenth-century Portuguese voyages and sugar colonies, with captives forced across the Middle Passage.
The triangular trade was a common pattern, not one fixed route.
Historians debate totals; the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database suggests about 12.5 million embarked and 10.7 million landed.
Plantation slavery in Brazil, the Caribbean and North America was chattel slavery, and enslaved people resisted through revolts, flight and everyday acts.
Abolition came by country: Britain in 1807 for the trade and 1833 for slavery, France 1848, the United States 1865, Brazil 1888.
Scholars disagree on the trade’s effects; Williams and Inikori stress economic links, while Drescher and others stress wider causes and moral politics.

en.title: European Overseas Expansion to 1800
en.short: Iberian voyages, maritime empires, chartered companies and the global links that shaped later imperialism.

sections.heading: Iberian voyages
sections.text: European overseas expansion began with Portugal and Castile, later Spain. Portugal explored the Atlantic coast of Africa and, under Vasco da Gama, reached India by sea in 1498. Castile sponsored Christopher Columbus, who reached the Caribbean in 1492. The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided non-European lands claimed by the two crowns. These voyages depended on improved ships, navigation and gunpowder weapons, but their purpose was trade, Christian mission and rivalry as much as curiosity.

sections.heading: Maritime empires
sections.text: Portugal built a maritime empire of fortified ports and factories, meaning trading posts, from East Africa to Asia. Spain conquered large American territories and organised them as viceroyalties, large territories ruled by royal viceroys. Both empires linked sea routes to land rule. They also created legal categories for conquered peoples and imported enslaved Africans, but the slave trade is treated separately in this course. Empire meant extraction of silver, sugar and spices, and it meant administration, garrisons and missionaries.

sections.heading: Trading companies
sections.text: In the seventeenth century the Dutch and English chartered companies became powerful. The Dutch East India Company (VOC, founded 1602) and the English East India Company (founded 1600) held monopoly privileges from their governments. A chartered company was a private body with public powers: it could trade, sign treaties, keep forts and raise troops. These companies pushed European influence into Asia through ports and alliances, often by force.

sections.heading: Global links and legacy
sections.text: Expansion tied four continents into one commercial system. The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia. Mercantilism, the idea that state power rested on trade and bullion, meaning gold and silver in bulk, encouraged colonies and rivalries. The resulting networks of forts, debts, treaties and naval bases, together with European claims to superiority, set conditions for nineteenth-century imperialism. They did not make it inevitable, but they supplied routes, capital, knowledge and habits of intervention.

keyPoints: Portugal and Castile led fifteenth-century oceanic voyages using improved ships and navigation.
The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided non-European claims between Portugal and Castile.
Maritime empires combined fortified ports, trading factories and colonial rule.
Chartered companies such as the VOC and English East India Company held monopoly privileges and public powers.
The Columbian Exchange linked the Americas with Afro-Eurasia through crops, animals, people and disease.
These networks created routes, capital and rivalries that helped make later imperialism possible.

en.title: The Early Modern World, 1500 to 1800: Empires, Silver and New Ideas
en.short: Five Asian empires, silver and crop flows, the Scientific Revolution, Enlightenment and Atlantic revolutions.

sections.heading: Three gunpowder empires
sections.text: The Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires are often called gunpowder empires, because artillery helped them centralise. The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and peaked under Suleiman (r. 1520-1566), ruling through sharia, sultanic law (kanun) and the devshirme, a levy of Christian boys trained for service in the administration and the janissary corps. The Safavids, founded by Ismail I in 1501, made Twelver Shi’ism Persia’s state religion. The Mughals began with Babur’s victory at Panipat in 1526; Akbar (r. 1556-1605) built a revenue system and practised religious accommodation, while Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) reimposed the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims.

sections.heading: East Asia
sections.text: Ming China (1368-1644) restored Chinese rule, ran civil service examinations and collected taxes in silver. The Manchu Qing (1644-1912) expanded under Kangxi and Qianlong and confined European trade to Canton. Tokugawa Japan (1603-1868) left emperors as figureheads; shoguns ruled from Edo, held lords to alternate attendance (sankin kotai) and restricted foreign trade mainly to Dutch and Chinese merchants at Nagasaki.

sections.heading: Silver and crops
sections.text: American silver from Potosí and Zacatecas drained towards China, which used it as money; the Manila galleons, sailing from 1565, carried much of it across the Pacific. The Columbian exchange carried maize, potato, sweet potato and cassava out of the Americas, and wheat, horses and smallpox in. Worked example: suppose gold trades at 12:1 with silver in Europe and 6:1 in China. Take 12 kg of silver to China, buy 2 kg of gold, sell it in Europe for 24 kg of silver. Gross gain 12 kg, or 100 per cent, before costs and risk. Real ratios varied.

sections.heading: New thought, new politics
sections.text: The Scientific Revolution replaced Aristotelian cosmology with mathematics and experiment: Copernicus (1543), Kepler’s ellipses, Galileo, Newton’s Principia (1687). The Enlightenment applied reason to society: Locke on consent, Montesquieu on separated powers, Rousseau on the general will, Diderot’s Encyclopédie. The Atlantic revolutions turned ideas into politics: American independence (1776), the French Revolution (1789), and Haiti’s revolution, which ended slavery and won independence in 1804.

keyPoints: The Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires rested on agrarian revenue, trade and gunpowder armies.
Ming and Qing China used silver as tax money; Qing confined European trade to Canton.
Tokugawa Japan was run by shoguns from Edo, with tight control of lords and foreign trade.
American silver reached China through the Manila galleons, linking the world economy.
The Columbian exchange moved crops and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia.
The Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment reshaped knowledge, and the Atlantic revolutions reshaped politics.

en.title: The Industrial Revolution and Social Change
en.short: Why British industry began, factories, towns, class conflict, reform, and Africa’s raw material trade.

sections.heading: Why Britain first
sections.text: Industrialisation means replacing hand work with machine production in large units. Britain led for several reasons. It had coal near iron and cheap canal transport. Its agriculture fed more people with fewer farm hands, pushing workers to towns. Overseas trade and colonial wealth supplied capital and markets. A wage economy meant people bought goods instead of making them. Skilled mechanics and patent law encouraged invention. No single cause explains it; historians debate the weight of empire and cotton.

sections.heading: Technology and the factory
sections.text: The key early technology was the cotton mill, using machines such as the spinning jenny and the water frame, later driven by James Watt’s improved steam engine. Smelting iron with coke, coal heated to drive off impurities, and after 1830 the railway, cut costs further. The factory gathered machines and workers under one roof and one clock, with supervision and discipline. Output per worker rose and cloth prices fell, so demand grew. The pattern later spread to iron, coal and engineering.

sections.heading: Towns and classes
sections.text: Towns grew faster than housing, water and drainage, so overcrowding and disease were common. Two classes became visible: the owners of mills and capital, and wage workers with little property. Workers responded with trade unions, long restricted by law, and with protest; the Luddites destroyed machines in England around 1811 to 1816. Reformers campaigned against child labour and long hours. Britain’s Factory Acts from 1833 limited child work and created inspectors, and the Chartists demanded the vote.

sections.heading: Africa and the trade
sections.text: Industrial Europe and North America needed raw materials and markets, drawing Africa into new trade. West African palm oil, groundnuts and cocoa, and later cotton and minerals, were exported in growing volume. Some African farmers and merchants gained, but payment was often in cheap manufactures. The search for raw materials and markets was one motive behind the colonial conquest of the late nineteenth century. Historians still argue how far industry caused imperialism and how far African economies were reshaped to serve it.

keyPoints: Industrialisation began in Britain through a combination of coal, transport, agricultural change, overseas capital and mechanical skill, not one single cause.
The factory system concentrated machines and workers under supervision, raising output per worker and lowering prices.
Urban growth outran housing and sanitation, producing overcrowding and disease.
Workers organised unions and protests such as the Luddites, while reformers won factory legislation from 1833 in Britain.
Industrial demand for raw materials tied Africa into export trade in palm oil, groundnuts, cocoa, cotton and minerals.
Historians disagree on how far industrial needs caused the colonial conquest of the late nineteenth century.

en.title: Colonialism and Imperialism in the Nineteenth Century
en.short: Definitions, motives for new imperialism, the Berlin Conference and the start of colonial rule in Africa.

sections.heading: Defining the terms
sections.text: Colonialism is the practice of one state acquiring, settling and governing another territory and its people. Imperialism is the wider policy or ideology of extending power, whether by formal colonies, protectorates, economic pressure or informal influence. Colonialism is therefore one form of imperialism, not a synonym. The 'new imperialism' of the late nineteenth century was rapid, competitive and mainly directed at Africa and Asia.

sections.heading: Motives for new imperialism
sections.text: Economic motives included the search for raw materials, markets and profitable investment outlets for industrial economies. Political motives included great-power rivalry, national prestige, strategic ports and routes, and the need to protect existing trade. Ideological motives included the civilising mission, missionary zeal, racism and social Darwinism, which wrongly ranked peoples as superior or inferior. Historians disagree on which motive mattered most. J. A. Hobson (1902) and V. I. Lenin (1916) stressed economic causes; others emphasise rivalry between officials, soldiers and traders on the ground.

sections.heading: Berlin and partition
sections.text: The Berlin Conference met in 1884 and 1885 at Bismarck’s invitation. No African rulers took part. It did not itself draw the map of Africa. It set rules for European claims, including notification of annexations and, in the Congo basin, free trade. The principle of effective occupation meant a power had to show it could administer what it claimed; this encouraged conquest. Bilateral treaties and later agreements completed the partition. The scramble was not a single event but a short, intense competition.

sections.heading: Establishing colonial rule
sections.text: Colonial rule was established by conquest, unequal treaties, protectorates and chartered companies, which were private firms granted state charters to trade and govern on the state’s behalf. A protectorate is a territory that keeps its own ruler but loses control of foreign and defence policy to the protecting power. In the Niger basin, the Royal Niger Company signed treaties with local rulers before Britain took over the company’s territories in 1900. Administrations used direct rule, indirect rule through local chiefs, or settler rule. Africans resisted in many places, but that is treated separately.

keyPoints: Colonialism is the acquisition and government of a dependent territory; imperialism is the broader extension of power.
The new imperialism was driven by economic, political and ideological motives, and historians weigh them differently.
J. A. Hobson and V. I. Lenin stressed economic causes, while other historians emphasise rivalry and local initiatives.
The Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 set rules for European claims but did not itself partition Africa.
Effective occupation and bilateral treaties turned claims into conquest and completed the scramble.
Colonial rule was imposed through conquest, unequal treaties, protectorates and chartered companies.

en.title: African Resistance to Colonial Conquest and Rule
en.short: Military, political and religious resistance to colonial conquest, with cases and debates on collaboration.

sections.heading: Forms of resistance
sections.text: Resistance means action to oppose, limit or overturn colonial control; collaboration means working with colonial authorities. Resistance took military forms, such as armies, guerrilla raids and sieges; political forms, such as refusing treaties, boycotts, rival administrations and exile; and religious forms, such as jihad, prophetic movements and defence of sacred authority. These forms often mixed. A rebellion could begin as a tax protest, gain a religious leader and end as a war of independence.

sections.heading: Cases of conquest
sections.text: Samori Ture built a Wassoulou state and fought French expansion in West Africa, using mobile columns and scorched earth before his capture in 1898. The Asante fought several British wars; in 1900 Yaa Asantewaa led resistance to the demand for the Golden Stool. At Adwa in 1896, Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu defeated an Italian army, preserving Ethiopian independence. The Maji Maji rising in German East Africa, 1905 to 1907, used maji, a medicine believed to protect fighters, and was crushed by famine and scorched earth. The Sokoto Caliphate, a jihad state, resisted British conquest until 1903, when its forces fell and the British kept emirs under indirect rule.

sections.heading: Why outcomes differed
sections.text: Outcomes depended on military technology, transport, terrain, the unity or division of African polities, diplomacy, external allies and timing. Ethiopia had a central state, large armies, imported arms and diplomatic skill. Samori Ture fought without a secure base. Maji Maji fighters mostly lacked firearms. Sokoto’s cavalry and walled cities could not match British machine guns. Local rivalries and famine also weakened resistance.

sections.heading: Collaboration and debate
sections.text: Nationalist historians often praised resisters and condemned collaborators as traitors. Later historians ask who collaborated, when and why: survival, trade, protection from rivals, coercion or belief that accommodation was wiser. They note that resistance could defend a local ruler rather than a nation, and that colonial rule was often established through African allies, soldiers and clerks. The debate now treats resistance and collaboration as shifting choices within unequal power, not simple moral labels.

keyPoints: Resistance to colonial conquest took military, political and religious forms, often combined.
Samori Ture fought French expansion until his capture in 1898; Asante resistance included the 1900 Yaa Asantewaa war.
Ethiopia preserved independence by defeating Italy at Adwa in 1896.
Maji Maji in German East Africa, 1905 to 1907, and the Sokoto Caliphate’s fall in 1903 show religious and political resistance crushed by superior force.
Outcomes depended on technology, logistics, terrain, unity, diplomacy and timing.
Historians now study collaboration as a shifting choice under unequal power, not simple betrayal.

en.title: Colonial Africa: Economy, Society and Administration
en.short: Direct and indirect rule, land, tax, migrant labour, cash crops and colonial social change.

sections.heading: Direct and indirect rule
sections.text: Direct rule meant government by officials from the colonial power, treating the colony as an extension of the home state. France used it, notably in the four communes of Senegal, and its policy of assimilation offered citizenship to a small educated minority. Indirect rule, linked to Frederick Lugard in Northern Nigeria and set out in The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922), governed through existing chiefs under British supervision. It was cheap, but it fixed chiefs in office and gave them new powers.

sections.heading: Land, tax and crops
sections.text: Colonial governments claimed 'waste' or unoccupied land as Crown or state land, though in much of West Africa most land stayed under African communal ownership. In settler colonies such as Kenya, Southern Rhodesia and Algeria it was sold or seized by Europeans, pushing Africans into crowded reserves or landlessness. Hut and poll taxes had to be paid in cash, so households sold crops or labour. Cash crops included cocoa in the Gold Coast, groundnuts in Senegal and northern Nigeria, cotton in Uganda and Sudan. Mines took gold and diamonds in South Africa and copper in Northern Rhodesia. A household owing 10 shillings in tax, with groundnuts at 5 shillings a bag, must sell two bags or send a man for wages.

sections.heading: Migrant labour
sections.text: Miners and plantations needed many cheap workers. The migrant labour system moved men, often for a year or more, from rural homes to distant mines, leaving women to farm. The South African gold mines drew workers from Mozambique, Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia into closed compounds, walled hostels where they lived under control. Chiefs and recruiting agencies supplied men under pressure. The mine gained a worker; the village lost a farmer.

sections.heading: Missions, schools and towns
sections.text: Missions ran most early schools, and literacy produced new elites: clerks, teachers, catechists, later lawyers and journalists. The Creoles of Sierra Leone, the évolués of French Africa and the assimilados of Portuguese Africa were small, privileged groups defined by education. Towns grew around ports, mines and administrative centres, such as Lagos, Accra, Nairobi and Dakar, with wage work, markets, newspapers and trade unions.

keyPoints: Direct rule used officials of the colonial power; indirect rule used existing chiefs under supervision.
Indirect rule is associated with Frederick Lugard in Northern Nigeria and his book The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922).
Colonial governments claimed unoccupied land as Crown or state land, and settler colonies sold or leased it to Europeans.
Taxes payable in cash forced Africans into wage labour or cash crop farming.
The migrant labour system moved men to mines and plantations for long periods, leaving women to farm.
Missions and schools created new educated elites, and towns grew around ports, mines and administrative centres.

en.title: Nationalism and Independence in Africa and Asia
en.short: Nationalist movements, elite and popular roles, and decolonisation paths in Ghana, Nigeria, India and beyond.

sections.heading: Nationalism rises
sections.text: Nationalism is a movement claiming self-rule for a colonial territory. It grew from colonial education, towns, newspapers, racial discrimination and economic grievance, and it was strengthened by the world wars. Educated elites, lawyers, teachers, journalists and some chiefs formed parties and newspapers. Workers used unions, strikes and boycotts. Women organised market protests, petitions and party wings. Veterans who had served in the world wars expected better treatment; in the Gold Coast a 1948 ex-servicemen’s march was fired on, and the unrest helped Kwame Nkrumah’s Convention People’s Party. Not every elite wanted immediate independence; some sought reform first.

sections.heading: Paths to independence
sections.text: Decolonisation is the transfer of sovereignty from a colonial power to a new state. Ghana took a negotiated path: Nkrumah’s party used strikes and non-cooperation, won elections and led the Gold Coast to independence in 1957. Nigeria’s nationalists built the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons, Action Group and Northern People’s Congress, but regional rivalry shaped a federal constitution before independence in 1960. India’s Indian National Congress, under Gandhi and Nehru, used mass civil disobedience; independence in 1947 came with partition into India and Pakistan. Elsewhere the path was armed struggle, as in Algeria and Kenya, or UN trusteeship and plebiscites. Forms included negotiated independence, partition, federation and Commonwealth membership.

sections.heading: Cold War setting
sections.text: The Cold War, the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union after 1945, shaped decolonisation. Nationalists could appeal for support from either superpower, while colonial powers claimed they were defending the free world. Some movements were socialist, some pro-Western, and many tried non-alignment, the policy of staying outside the blocs. The Bandung Conference of 1955 and the Non-Aligned Movement from 1961 gave that idea a voice. Cold War pressure sometimes hastened independence and sometimes produced proxy conflict or coups after it. Local protest remained the main force; superpower rivalry changed the opportunities and dangers.

keyPoints: Nationalism claimed self-rule and drew on colonial education, towns, the press, economic grievance and the world wars.
Elites formed parties, workers struck, women organised, and veterans’ protests exposed colonial injustice.
Ghana reached independence in 1957 through Nkrumah’s Convention People’s Party and negotiated elections.
Nigeria’s regional parties and federal constitution shaped independence in 1960, while India’s Congress won independence in 1947 with partition.
Decolonisation took negotiated, armed, partitioned, federal and trusteeship forms.
Cold War rivalry and non-alignment shaped opportunities, but local pressure drove decolonisation.

en.title: Nigeria: Peoples, States and Colonial Formation
en.short: Precolonial Nigerian peoples and states, British conquest and 1914 amalgamation, regionalism and independence in 1960.

sections.heading: Precolonial peoples and states
sections.text: The area that became Nigeria held many societies, not one nation. In the north, Hausa city-states and Kanem-Bornu linked trans-Saharan trade; the Sokoto Caliphate, founded in the early nineteenth century, became a large Islamic state. In the west, Oyo and Benin were powerful kingdoms. Igbo communities often governed through councils and age grades rather than kings, while Niger Delta city-states grew on Atlantic trade. These units differed in language, religion and political scale.

sections.heading: Conquest and amalgamation
sections.text: British influence began from Lagos and the coast and expanded by treaty, trade and force. The Royal Niger Company administered much of the Niger area until 1900, when Britain took direct control. In 1914 the Northern Protectorate and the Colony and Protectorate of Southern Nigeria were amalgamated into one colony and protectorate, mainly for administrative and financial convenience. Amalgamation means joining separate administrations under one government. Indirect rule, governing through recognised chiefs and emirs, was used, but it fitted some societies better than others.

sections.heading: Regions and tensions
sections.text: By the 1950s the colonial state was federal in practice, with three regions: Northern, Western and Eastern, later joined by a Mid-Western Region. Regional governments had strong powers, and each drew on a different ethnic and political base. The North had a larger population and fewer Western-style schools; the South had earlier missionary schooling and a stronger export economy. Revenue allocation, minority fears and competition for jobs fed tension. Political parties also had regional roots, such as the NPC in the North, the Action Group in the West and the NCNC, strongest in the East.

sections.heading: Road to independence
sections.text: Constitutional reforms after the Second World War widened representation. The Richards Constitution of 1946 created regional assemblies; the Macpherson Constitution of 1951 and the Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 increased elected representation and regional self-government. Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 as a federation, and a republic in 1963. The new state inherited strong regions and weak national unity, so disputes over power, revenue and identity shaped its early politics.

keyPoints: The area that became Nigeria contained many societies and states, not a single precolonial nation.
British rule expanded from Lagos and the coast and was consolidated by the 1914 amalgamation.
Indirect rule governed through recognised chiefs and emirs but worked unevenly across societies.
The colonial federation gave strong powers to the Northern, Western and Eastern Regions.
Regional parties, uneven schooling and revenue disputes created tensions at independence.
Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 and a republic in 1963.

en.title: Postcolonial Africa: States, Crises and Reform
en.short: Military rule, one-party states, economic crisis, democratisation, civil wars, AU and governance debates.

sections.heading: Independence and state power
sections.text:
At independence, new states inherited colonial boundaries and export economies. Many leaders chose one-party rule, arguing that multiparty competition would divide young nations; critics say it narrowed participation. Military coups became common from the 1960s. Soldiers promised to end corruption, but military governments abused rights and delayed civilian rule.

Neopatrimonialism describes formal institutions working through personal patronage, where leaders reward allies with jobs and contracts. It explains weak accountability in some states, not all.

sections.heading: Economic crisis and adjustment
sections.text:
Economic decline had many causes: dependence on few exports, falling prices, oil shocks, borrowing, drought, conflict and policy errors. By the 1980s many governments faced debt. Structural adjustment programmes (SAPs), backed by the IMF and World Bank, offered loans on conditions such as privatisation, trade liberalisation, devaluation and cuts to public spending. Supporters say SAPs stabilised economies; critics say they raised prices and cut health and education.

If a currency falls from 100 to 200 units per dollar, a 10-dollar import rises from 1,000 to 2,000 units, a 100% increase.

sections.heading: Conflict and regional bodies
sections.text:
Civil wars caused severe suffering in Nigeria (1967 to 1970), Sudan, Angola, Mozambique, Liberia, Sierra Leone, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda. Causes included colonial legacies, regional inequality, weak states and external intervention.

The Organisation of African Unity, founded in 1963, avoided interfering in members’ internal affairs. Its successor, the African Union (AU), founded in 2002, allows intervention in grave cases and runs a Peace and Security Council. Regional bodies include ECOWAS, SADC, the EAC and IGAD.

sections.heading: Democratisation and debates
sections.text:
From the 1990s, multiparty elections spread after the Cold War. Many produced real change; others produced hybrid regimes, where elections coexist with repression. Term limits and electoral commissions are central issues.

Current debates ask whether African states are weak or merely poorly governed, how to reduce corruption and commodity dependence, and how to manage youth, cities, climate and digital change. Recent coups in West Africa and the Sahel have renewed debate about democracy and security.

keyPoints: One-party rule and military coups were common after independence, often justified by unity or order but criticised for narrowing participation.
Economic decline came from commodity dependence, debt, shocks, conflict and policy, and SAPs attached conditions to loans.
Civil wars had multiple causes including colonial legacies, inequality, weak states and external intervention.
The OAU avoided internal interference; the AU permits intervention in grave cases and has a Peace and Security Council.
Democratisation from the 1990s produced both real transitions and hybrid regimes.
Current debates focus on state capacity, corruption, commodity dependence, youth, climate and security, with recent coups renewing concern.

en.title: The Two World Wars and the Interwar World
en.short: Causes, course and settlement of the two world wars, the Holocaust, and the 1945 order.

sections.heading: The First World War
sections.text: The First World War grew from rival alliance blocs, imperial rivalry, an arms race and Balkan nationalism. The trigger was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July; alliances drew in Russia, Germany, France and Britain. Fighting became trench warfare on the Western Front. It was total war, mobilising industry and civilians. Russia left after the 1917 revolutions; the United States entered that year. Germany signed an armistice on 11 November 1918.

sections.heading: Peace and interwar crisis
sections.text: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany, cut its territory and armed forces and imposed reparations, which Germans resented. The League of Nations had little power to enforce decisions, and the United States never joined. The Depression from 1929 brought mass unemployment. Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany rose; Hitler became chancellor in 1933. Britain and France chose appeasement, conceding at Munich in 1938. The settlement did not build a stable order.

sections.heading: The Second World War
sections.text: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Blitzkrieg, or fast combined attack, brought quick victories; the 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union and the attack on Pearl Harbor made it a world war. Stalingrad (1942-43) marked the turning point. The Holocaust was the Nazi genocide of about six million Jews, and also of Roma, disabled people and others, through ghettos, mass shootings and camps such as Auschwitz. Germany surrendered in May 1945, Japan in September, after the atomic bombs.

sections.heading: Empires and the 1945 order
sections.text: The war ended Europe’s global dominance. Japan’s occupations in Asia undermined claims of European superiority and strengthened independence movements; India became independent in 1947. In Africa, conscription, forced labour and inflation bred grievance, while the 1941 Atlantic Charter raised expectations of self-rule. The 1945 United Nations gave great powers vetoes; Bretton Woods set up the IMF and World Bank. Nuremberg trials and the 1948 Genocide Convention and Universal Declaration of Human Rights tried to place law above states. Europe soon divided into Cold War blocs.

keyPoints: The First World War began as a Balkan dispute between Austria-Hungary and Serbia and became general through the alliance system.
The Treaty of Versailles blamed Germany and imposed reparations, while the League of Nations could not enforce peace.
Appeasement failed; Germany invaded Poland in September 1939 and the war became global in 1941.
The Holocaust was the Nazi genocide of about six million Jews and of other groups such as Roma and disabled people.
The war weakened European empires and accelerated independence in Asia and Africa.
The 1945 settlement created the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions, and was soon split by the Cold War.

en.title: The Cold War and the Post Cold War World
en.short: Origins, phases and end of the US-Soviet Cold War, its proxy conflicts, and the post-1991 global order.

sections.heading: Origins
sections.text:
The Cold War was the long rivalry between the United States and its allies and the Soviet Union and its allies. It was fought through ideology, arms, alliances and proxy wars, not direct war. Its roots lie in the 1917 Russian Revolution, Western fear of communist expansion, and the collapse after 1945 of the wartime alliance.

Key markers: the Truman Doctrine (1947), promising to contain Soviet expansion; the Marshall Plan (1947); the Berlin Blockade (1948-49); NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955).

sections.heading: Phases and proxy wars
sections.text:
