Phases: confrontation from the late 1940s; détente (relaxation) in the late 1960s and 1970s, marked by SALT I (1972) and the Helsinki Accords (1975); renewed confrontation after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979; and the final phase under Gorbachev from 1985.

Nuclear risk pushed rivalry into proxy wars and interventions: Korea (1950-53), Vietnam and Afghanistan in Asia; Cuba, Chile (1973) and Nicaragua in Latin America; in Africa, the Congo crisis, Angola and Mozambique.

In Angola, independence in 1975 became a war between the Soviet- and Cuban-backed MPLA and UNITA, backed by South Africa and the United States.

sections.heading: The end
sections.text: Gorbachev’s glasnost (openness) and perestroika (economic restructuring) loosened party control and eased pressure on Eastern Europe. Revolutions swept the region in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell that November, Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991. Economic strain, the arms race and rising nationalism in the republics contributed.

sections.heading: After 1991
sections.text:
The order after 1991 was briefly unipolar, with the United States dominant. Fukuyama’s 'end of history' (1989) claimed liberal democracy had triumphed; Huntington (1993) predicted a clash of civilisations.

Globalisation is the growing cross-border flow of goods, capital, people and information. Hyperglobalists see a borderless world economy; sceptics reply that trade is concentrated in regional blocs and states remain strong; transformationalists see both.

The World Trade Organization was created in 1995. Critics link globalisation to inequality and Africa’s marginalisation; supporters credit it with growth and poverty reduction.

keyPoints: The Cold War was a US-Soviet rivalry fought through alliances, arms races and proxy wars rather than direct war.
Containment, the policy of limiting Soviet expansion, shaped the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan.
Détente eased tension in the 1970s, but the 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan renewed confrontation.
Gorbachev’s glasnost and perestroika, with the 1989 revolutions in Eastern Europe, preceded the Soviet dissolution of December 1991.
The post-1991 order was briefly unipolar, and Fukuyama and Huntington offered rival predictions about it.
Hyperglobalists, sceptics and transformationalists disagree on how far globalisation erodes state power and reduces poverty.

en.title: History of International Relations and Diplomacy
en.short: State systems, diplomacy, treaties and international law from Westphalia to the UN.

sections.heading: States and congresses
sections.text:
The Peace of Westphalia (1648) ended the Thirty Years’ War. It is often taken as a marker for a European system of sovereign territorial states, though the change was gradual.

After the Napoleonic wars, the Congress of Vienna (1814-15) led to the Concert of Europe. Great powers met in congresses to manage disputes and keep a balance of power, meaning no state or alliance should dominate the rest. The Concert weakened after the Crimean War and collapsed by 1914.

sections.heading: Diplomacy at work
sections.text:
Diplomacy is the conduct of relations between states by negotiation, representation and information gathering. A foreign ministry directs policy; an ambassador heads a resident mission abroad and speaks for the sending state.

Diplomats negotiate treaties, which are binding written agreements governed in part by the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969). They report on the host country and protect citizens. Multilateral diplomacy at conferences and organisations depends on coalitions and drafting.

sections.heading: League and UN
sections.text:
The League of Nations was created in 1920 after the First World War to keep peace through collective security, the idea that aggression against one member concerns all. It lacked the United States, had weak enforcement powers and could not stop Japanese, Italian and German expansion in the 1930s.

The United Nations, founded in 1945, has a General Assembly of all members and a Security Council with five permanent members holding a veto. The Secretariat administers it, and the International Court of Justice hears state disputes.

sections.heading: Law and balance
sections.text:
International law rests mainly on treaties, customary practice accepted as law, and general principles. It governs diplomacy, war, trade and human rights, but enforcement is uneven because states consent to jurisdiction.

The balance of power is a policy and a description: states form alliances or build defences to prevent domination. In the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, public warnings, secret letters and UN talks helped the United States and Soviet Union avoid war.

keyPoints: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) is a marker for sovereign territorial states, though the change was gradual.
The Concert of Europe used great-power congresses and the balance of power after 1815.
Diplomats negotiate treaties, represent their states and report through foreign ministries.
The League of Nations (1920) used collective security but lacked the United States and strong enforcement.
The United Nations (1945) has a General Assembly and a Security Council with five permanent veto members.
International law rests on treaties and custom, but enforcement depends heavily on state consent.

en.title: Foreign Policy of African States
en.short: How African states make foreign policy, non-alignment, Pan-Africanism, regional bodies and Nigeria’s case.

sections.heading: Making foreign policy
sections.text:
Foreign policy is the set of goals and actions a state takes towards other states and international bodies. It is made through the executive, foreign ministry, legislature, security agencies and sometimes parties and public opinion.

Interests usually include security, sovereignty, economic development, prestige and solidarity with other Africans. Constraints include weak economies, dependence on commodity exports or aid, colonial ties, disputed borders, domestic conflict and limited information. Policy is therefore a process of bargaining, not a single decision.

sections.heading: Non-alignment and unity
sections.text:
Non-alignment means refusing to join the Cold War military blocs while trading and accepting aid from both sides. Leaders such as Nasser, Nkrumah and Nyerere used it to protect independence. Pan-Africanism is the belief in African unity and solidarity. It shaped the Organisation of African Unity in 1963 and the African Union in 2002, and supported liberation struggles, but sovereignty and rivalries limited unity.

Regional bodies such as ECOWAS (1975), SADC and the EAC coordinate trade, security and diplomacy. They give small states a voice but also constrain them.

sections.heading: Comparing African states
sections.text:
African states differ. Regional powers such as Nigeria, South Africa and Egypt act beyond their borders. Smaller or poorer states rely more on regional bodies and external donors. Former French colonies in particular keep close ties with Paris; many former British colonies keep looser links with Britain through the Commonwealth. Some states stress neutralism; others align with a great power.

Common aims are sovereignty, development, security and African solidarity, but capacity and domestic politics decide how far they are pursued.

sections.heading: Nigeria as a case
sections.text:
Nigeria is a case. Its policy is often called Afrocentric: support for decolonisation and anti-apartheid, regional peacekeeping and economic diplomacy. In 1990, Nigeria was the largest contributor to ECOMOG, the ECOWAS monitoring group sent into Liberia’s civil war.

Oil wealth, population and military weight give Nigeria influence. Yet dependence on oil, domestic instability, corruption and limited capacity constrain it. Nigeria shows both ambition and the limits of African foreign policy.

keyPoints: Foreign policy is shaped by interests such as security and development, and by constraints such as weak economies and colonial ties.
Non-alignment meant staying out of Cold War military blocs, not isolation from trade or aid.
Pan-Africanism inspired the OAU and AU and liberation solidarity, but sovereignty limited unity.
Regional bodies such as ECOWAS coordinate policy and give small states a voice.
Nigeria’s Afrocentric policy combines anti-colonial solidarity, peacekeeping and economic diplomacy.
Nigeria’s influence is limited by oil dependence, domestic instability and capacity.

en.title: International Organisations and Global Governance
en.short: The UN system, African Union and regional communities, WTO, peacekeeping, aid and governance limits.

sections.heading: UN system
sections.text:
The United Nations was founded in 1945. Its main organs include the General Assembly, where each member state has one vote; the Security Council, whose five permanent members hold a veto, the power to block a resolution (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States); the Economic and Social Council; the International Court of Justice; and the Secretariat.

Specialised agencies such as the World Health Organization and funds such as UNICEF form the wider UN system.

sections.heading: African institutions
sections.text:
The African Union replaced the Organisation of African Unity in 2002. It has 55 member states and works through an Assembly of heads of state, a Commission and a Peace and Security Council.

It recognises regional economic communities, groups of states that lower trade barriers and coordinate policy, such as ECOWAS in West Africa, SADC in southern Africa and the EAC in East Africa. These communities handle trade, migration and some peace work, but depend heavily on member subscriptions and outside donors.

sections.heading: Peacekeeping and aid
sections.text:
UN peacekeeping rests on consent of the parties, impartiality and force only in self-defence or defence of the mandate. It is not named in the UN Charter. African-led operations, such as the African Union Mission in Somalia from 2007, often rely on UN funding and logistics.

Humanitarian action follows humanity, impartiality, neutrality and independence. OCHA coordinates UN relief, and clusters group agencies by sector. The 1994 Rwanda genocide and 1995 Srebrenica massacre exposed failures of protection.

sections.heading: WTO and limits
sections.text:
Global governance means the rules and institutions through which states manage problems. The World Trade Organization began in 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. It administers trade rules, hosts negotiations and settles disputes. Its highest body is the Ministerial Conference; decisions are by consensus.

Governance is limited by sovereignty, great-power interests and weak enforcement. The Security Council veto can block action. The WTO Appellate Body has not heard new appeals since 2019 because the United States blocked appointments.

keyPoints: Global governance is the rules and institutions through which states manage shared problems, but it is not world government.
The UN Security Council has five permanent members with veto power, which can block action.
The African Union, founded in 2002, works with regional economic communities such as ECOWAS, SADC and the EAC.
UN peacekeeping requires consent, impartiality and limited force, and it is not named in the UN Charter.
Humanitarian action follows humanity, impartiality, neutrality and independence, with OCHA coordinating UN relief.
The WTO administers trade rules and dispute settlement, but its Appellate Body has not heard new appeals since 2019.

en.title: Foundations of Public International Law
en.short: Sources, subjects, sovereignty, recognition, state responsibility, treaties, ICJ, law of the sea and humanitarian law.

sections.heading: Sources and subjects
sections.text: Public international law governs relations between states and other international actors. Article 38(1) of the Statute of the International Court of Justice lists treaties, customary international law and general principles as sources. Custom needs general state practice accepted as law. Judicial decisions and writers are subsidiary. States are the main subjects; international organisations and individuals have limited personality.

sections.heading: Sovereignty and responsibility
sections.text: Sovereignty is a state’s authority over its territory and people, and its equality with other states. Non-intervention protects it, but international law limits how states treat people and use force. Recognition acknowledges that an entity is a state or that a government represents one. The declaratory view says it confirms facts; the constitutive view says it creates statehood. State responsibility arises when conduct attributable to a state breaches an obligation; the state must cease and make reparation.

sections.heading: Treaties and the ICJ
sections.text: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 codifies treaty law. A treaty is a written agreement between states governed by international law. Pacta sunt servanda means agreements bind in good faith. The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations. It hears disputes between states only, with consent, and gives advisory opinions to authorised United Nations bodies.

sections.heading: Sea and humanitarian law
sections.text: The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea 1982 sets sea zones: territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles, exclusive economic zone up to 200, and high seas. International humanitarian law applies in armed conflict. The Geneva Conventions 1949 and Additional Protocols protect wounded soldiers, prisoners and civilians. Principles include distinction, proportionality and humane treatment. Example: if state A’s soldiers enter state B without consent and damage a school, A is responsible. It must cease and make reparation.

keyPoints: Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute lists treaties, custom and general principles as the main sources of international law.
States are the primary subjects of international law; international organisations and individuals have limited legal personality.
Sovereignty gives a state authority over its territory and equality with other states, but it is limited by international law.
Recognition may be declaratory, confirming facts, or constitutive, creating statehood; the two theories disagree.
State responsibility requires conduct attributable to a state and a breach of an international obligation, followed by cessation and reparation.
The Vienna Convention 1969 governs treaties, the ICJ decides state disputes with consent, and the 1982 Law of the Sea Convention and the Geneva Conventions set rules for the sea and armed conflict.

en.title: International Political Economy and Development
en.short: Trade, finance, aid, debt, multinational firms, rival views, development theory and global institutions.

sections.heading: The global economy
sections.text: International political economy (IPE) studies how politics and markets interact across borders. Trade is the exchange of goods and services. Finance covers cross-border loans, investment and currency flows. Aid is a transfer on concessional (softer than market) terms, often official development assistance (ODA), meaning grants or low-interest loans from governments. Debt is money borrowed and repayable with interest. Multinational firms own or control production in more than one country.

sections.heading: Three perspectives
sections.text: Liberals see trade, finance and foreign investment as mutually beneficial, following comparative advantage, the idea that each country gains by producing what it makes relatively best. They accept aid for poverty relief and argue that open markets and sound institutions promote growth. Mercantilists, or economic nationalists, stress state power. They seek trade surpluses, protect strategic industries, tie aid to political aims and treat multinationals as national instruments. Structuralists see a hierarchy of core and periphery. They argue that primary-commodity exporters face weak and unstable prices, that debt and multinationals can drain surplus, and that aid may carry conditions that limit policy space.

sections.heading: Development theories
sections.text: Modernisation theory expects growth through investment, education and institutions. Dependency theory says peripheral economies are shaped by their links to richer cores. Import substitution protects domestic industry; export-led growth uses foreign markets. Neoliberalism favours privatisation, liberalisation and fiscal discipline. The human development approach measures wellbeing by health, education and income. Structural adjustment was a set of conditional IMF and World Bank lending policies in the 1980s and 1990s, and critics said it cut social spending.

sections.heading: Institutions and case
sections.text: The IMF lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems, meaning a shortage of foreign currency to pay for imports and debts. The World Bank funds development projects and policy loans. The WTO administers trade rules; GATT preceded it. Consider an invented case: Aminata’s country exports cocoa and imports machines. A fall in cocoa prices worsens its trade balance, so it borrows. If the loan is used for machinery that raises cocoa output, debt may be sustainable; if it pays salaries, repayment is harder. This shows why trade, finance and debt are linked.

keyPoints: International political economy studies the interaction of states, markets and power across borders.
Liberals stress mutual gains from trade, investment and open markets.
Mercantilists stress state power, trade surpluses and strategic industries.
Structuralists stress core-periphery inequality, weak commodity prices and surplus drain.
Development theories include modernisation, dependency, import substitution, export-led growth and human development.
The IMF, World Bank and WTO manage payments support, development finance and trade rules.

en.title: Peace, Conflict and Security Studies
en.short: Conflict causes and types, negotiation, mediation, peacebuilding, and national, human and collective security.

sections.heading: Conflict and causes
sections.text: Conflict is a disagreement or struggle between parties who perceive incompatible interests, needs or values. It can be interpersonal, communal, intra-state or interstate, and violent or non-violent. Structural conflict arises from unequal institutions, such as exclusion from land or jobs. Causes often combine competition for resources, weak institutions, identity grievances, power struggles and mistrust. Causes explain why conflict starts; resolution is the process of ending it and changing the relationships behind it. A ceasefire may stop fighting without resolving causes.

sections.heading: Resolving conflict
sections.text: Negotiation is direct bargaining between parties. Mediation uses a neutral third party who helps them communicate and propose options but does not impose a settlement. Conciliation is similar but often more advisory. Peacebuilding is longer-term work: rebuilding institutions, justice, reconciliation and livelihoods so violence does not return. Peacemaking seeks a settlement, while peacekeeping deploys personnel to monitor ceasefires. Resolution is not always agreement; it may require addressing grievances and guaranteeing safety.

sections.heading: Approaches to security
sections.text: National security focuses on protecting the state, its borders and sovereignty, mainly through military and intelligence means. Human security shifts attention to people: freedom from fear (violence) and freedom from want (poverty, hunger, disease). Collective security holds that aggression against one member concerns all, and members may act together, as under the United Nations Charter. These approaches can conflict: heavy state security may harm human security.

sections.heading: African regional bodies
sections.text: African regional bodies carry much peace and security work. The African Union has a Peace and Security Council and may authorise peace support operations. ECOWAS in West Africa, SADC in Southern Africa and IGAD in East Africa mediate disputes, send monitors and issue early warnings. In The Gambia in 2017, ECOWAS mediation and pressure helped resolve a post-election standoff after Yahya Jammeh refused to accept defeat. Such bodies depend on member states’ money and political will.

keyPoints: Conflict causes explain why conflict starts; resolution is the process of ending it and addressing underlying relationships.
Negotiation is direct bargaining; mediation adds a neutral third party who does not impose a decision.
Peacebuilding is long-term work on institutions, justice and livelihoods to prevent renewed violence.
National security protects the state; human security protects people from fear and want.
Collective security treats aggression against one member as a concern for all members.
African regional bodies such as the AU, ECOWAS, SADC and IGAD mediate, keep peace and give early warning.

en.title: Research Methods and the Long Essay in History
en.short: Choosing a question, reviewing literature, archival and field work, notes, citation, and writing the long essay.

sections.heading: Topic and question
sections.text: Start with a topic you can handle with available sources and time. Narrow it into a research question: a clear, answerable question, not a broad label. “How did market women in one Nigerian town respond to price controls in the 1940s?” is workable; “Women in colonial Nigeria” is not. Write a provisional thesis, the argument you will test, and be ready to change it. Check with your supervisor early.

sections.heading: Reading and sources
sections.text: Build a literature review by reading what scholars have already argued, then grouping their positions and identifying a gap. Keep full bibliographic details from the first reading. In an archive, plan visits, register, note collection and file references, and respect rules on photography and copying. In the field, prepare questions, seek informed consent, record interviews with permission, and store data safely. Distinguish primary sources, made at the time, from secondary sources, later interpretations.

sections.heading: Notes and ethics
sections.text: Take notes in one consistent system. For every note record author, title, date, page or file, and whether it is quotation, paraphrase or your own comment. Paraphrase in your own words and use quotation marks for exact words. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words or ideas as yours. Cite every borrowed fact or interpretation in the style your department requires, such as a recognised author-date or note system, and list all sources in the bibliography.

sections.heading: Writing and presenting
sections.text: Most history long essays have an introduction stating the question and thesis; a literature review; a section on sources and method; analytical chapters in chronological or thematic order; a conclusion answering the question; and a bibliography. Write in clear paragraphs, one main point each. Draft early, revise for argument and evidence, then proofread. Follow the department’s rules on length, font, margins, referencing and submission. Prepare a short oral presentation: state your question, method, main findings and limits.

keyPoints: A good long essay starts from a narrow, answerable research question and a provisional thesis.
A literature review groups existing arguments and identifies the gap your study addresses.
Record full source details and page or file references for every note you take.
Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words or ideas as your own; cite all borrowed material in the required style.
The essay should move from question and method through analysis to a conclusion that answers the question.
Follow departmental formatting rules and prepare a clear oral presentation.

en.title: Advanced Historiography and Historical Theory
en.short: Annales, Marxist, nationalist and postcolonial theory, and debates on structure, agency, narrative and evidence.

sections.heading: Major schools
sections.text: Theory decides what a historian treats as a problem. The Annales school, begun by Lucien Febvre and Marc Bloch in 1929, favoured long-term social patterns, the longue durée, and later mentalités, shared mentalities. Marxist historiography uses historical materialism, the view that material production and class relations shape change, though E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm avoided crude determinism. Nationalist historiography, prominent in decolonising Africa, recovered African agency and state formation against colonial belittlement. Postcolonial theory, linked to Edward Said, Subaltern Studies and Dipesh Chakrabarty, examines how colonial knowledge and categories such as race shaped rule and history writing. Each school asks different questions of the same archive.

sections.heading: Structure, narrative, evidence
sections.text: Structure and agency is the debate over whether enduring social relations or human choices explain events. Structures include class, gender and colonial administration; agency is people’s capacity to act and resist. Anthony Giddens’s structuration theory holds that structures both constrain and are reproduced by action. Hayden White argued in Metahistory (1973) that historians impose a narrative form, or emplotment, on the past. This does not make evidence optional: evidence is the surviving trace that can confirm, qualify or refute a story. Carlo Ginzburg’s microhistory shows how close reading of small records can test large claims. Narrative shapes explanation, but evidence limits it.

sections.heading: Theory at work
sections.text: Take the 1929 Aba Women’s Protest in southeastern Nigeria. A nationalist historian may ask how it expressed anti-colonial resistance. A Marxist may stress colonial taxation and warrant chiefs. An Annales historian may study market women’s networks and mentalités. A postcolonial historian may ask how gender and colonial categories shaped the protest and its records. Theory changes the question, the sources chosen and the explanation offered. The test remains: does the evidence support the claim?

keyPoints: The Annales school studies long-term structures and mentalités rather than events alone.
Marxist historiography explains change through material production and class relations, but avoids crude determinism.
Nationalist and postcolonial historians recover agency and expose colonial categories.
The structure and agency debate asks how far enduring social relations and human choices explain events.
Hayden White showed that narrative shapes history, while evidence still tests and limits the story.
Theory changes the questions historians ask, the sources they select and the explanations they offer.

en.title: Designing and Writing the Master’s Dissertation
en.short: Research design, proposals, source criticism, archives, ethics, writing, supervision and the viva.

sections.heading: From question to design
sections.text: A dissertation is a supervised, examinable piece of independent research. Start with one clear research question that your sources can answer and your literature review shows is worth asking. Research design is the plan linking question, concepts, evidence and method. The proposal states the problem, question, objectives, literature gap, sources, methods, ethics and chapter outline. Check feasibility: archive access, language, time and ethics approval. Rules and word limits vary by university and country, so read the current handbook.

sections.heading: Source criticism and archives
sections.text: Advanced source criticism asks who made a document, for whom, why, when and from what information. Check authenticity, provenance (its chain of ownership), internal consistency, genre, audience and silence (what the record leaves out). Archival method means using finding aids, registers and catalogues to locate fonds (record groups), series and files. Record call numbers, dates and exact references. Compare documents with oral history, newspapers and official reports. In a hypothetical case, Amina studies market women’s petitions in a Nigerian city in the 1940s. She must confirm the archive holds the files, read them against officials’ reports, and interview those who remember the period, or descendants, only with consent.

sections.heading: Ethics with people
sections.text: Research with human subjects needs free, informed consent: people must understand the purpose, risks, benefits and their right to withdraw. Protect privacy and anonymity unless a participant agrees to be named. Store data securely and avoid harm or undue pressure. Oral history raises memory and ownership questions; let narrators check transcripts where possible. Ethics committees apply national and institutional rules, which differ, so follow your university’s current policy and local permits.

sections.heading: Writing, supervision, examination
sections.text: Write early and often. Keep a research log and reference manager. Draft chapters for your supervisor, who advises but does not write the thesis. Agree a schedule of meetings and written feedback. The dissertation is examined, often by internal and external examiners, with a viva voce (oral defence). Examiners judge the question, sources, argument, originality and presentation. Expect corrections. Length, submission rules and examination format vary by country and institution, so check regulations.

keyPoints: A master’s dissertation is independent research assessed by examiners, often through a viva voce; rules vary by university and country.
A strong proposal links one answerable research question to a feasible design, sources, methods, ethics and chapter plan.
Advanced source criticism tests provenance, authenticity, context, audience and silence, and corroborates documents with other evidence.
Archival method uses finding aids and careful citation of fonds, series, files and call numbers.
Research with human subjects requires informed consent, privacy, secure data and ethics approval.
Supervisors advise and comment, but the student must write the thesis and respond to examiners’ corrections.

en.title: Specialist Seminar: Frontiers in Historical and International Studies
en.short: Reading recent scholarship, reviewing debates, finding gaps and presenting seminar work.

sections.heading: Choosing a field
sections.text: A specialist seminar asks you to enter a live field. Fields include Atlantic history, the study of connections around the Atlantic Ocean; global history, which compares and connects regions; migration; gender; environment; and African political economy, the study of production, distribution and power in African economies. Choose a field narrow enough for a semester but tied to a real debate. Read recent articles and review essays. Note the central question, main positions, evidence and methods. A field map shows who argues with whom.

sections.heading: Reviewing a debate
sections.text: Do not summarise articles one by one. Group them by question or position. Ask where they agree, where they disagree, and whether the disagreement concerns facts, theory, sources or method. Check the date and place of each claim. A debate in one country or period may not travel unchanged. Write a short review that states the problem, explains two or three positions fairly and judges their evidence. This is a literature review, a critical account of existing scholarship, not a list.

sections.heading: Finding a gap
sections.text: A gap is a weakness or opening in the debate: a missing case, an untested claim, a silent group, an unused source or an untried method. It is not enough to say nobody has written on a place. Show why the gap matters. Imagine a student studying migration between northern Nigeria and Ghana. Recent studies focus on male labour migrants. She asks how women traders built networks and how that changes ideas of migration. That is a new question, not merely a new topic.

sections.heading: Presenting work
sections.text: Present original work as a seminar paper: a clear question, a short review of the debate, your argument, evidence and limits. Originality can come from a new source, comparison, method or interpretation. Keep the paper short and leave time for questions. Invite criticism and record it. After the seminar, revise the question and evidence later. This cycle, from reading to argument to peer review, is the core of master’s level work.

keyPoints: A specialist seminar requires entering a live scholarly debate in a narrow field.
A literature review groups scholarship by question and position, not by article.
A research gap is a problem in evidence, method, theory or coverage, not just an unstudied place.
Originality can come from new sources, comparisons, methods or interpretations.
A seminar paper needs a clear question, fair review, argument, evidence and limits.
Peer criticism should be recorded and used to revise the work.
